query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an initially single‐phase high-entropy alloy, sustained high-temperature or cyclic mechanical loading induces local atomic segregation that triggers the nucleation of nanoscale, brittle intermetallic precipitates (e.g., Laves or B2 phases) at dislocation cell boundaries and incipient grain boundaries. Although the high configurational entropy suppresses extensive grain coarsening and intergranular precipitation seen in conventional alloys, once these localized precipitates form they concentrate stress and promote brittle fracture.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-processed, compositionally homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloy (e.g., equiatomic FCC or BCC structure) with minimal nanoscale ordering or precipitates.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to accelerated aging via prolonged high-temperature exposure and/or cyclic mechanical loading at service-relevant conditions.
generation.conditions: Elevated service temperatures (e.g., 600–900 °C) and cyclic loading environments that mimic prolonged operational stresses; tests performed under inert or controlled atmospheres to isolate thermal and mechanical effects.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale brittle precipitates that nucleate at dislocation network sites and incipient grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Under sustained thermal and mechanical stresses, local fluctuations in composition overcome kinetic barriers, leading to the nucleation of ordered intermetallic phases within the uniform matrix. These precipitates, even at low volume fractions, act as internal stress concentrators and reduce the alloy's capacity for plastic deformation, thereby degrading toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the pristine alloy, the aged or cyclically loaded alloy will exhibit a marked reduction in toughness (e.g., lower fracture strain or Charpy impact energy) while possibly maintaining or even increasing yield strength. Microstructural analysis (TEM/atom-probe tomography) will reveal emergent nanoscale precipitates at dislocation boundaries that are absent in the baseline material.
generation.baseline: The as-processed, single-phase high-entropy alloy without detectable nanoscale segregation or precipitate formation.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected under sustained high-temperature and cyclic loading conditions typical of demanding engineering service; under lower temperatures or short-term loading, the alloy should retain its high toughness.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the precise kinetics, volume fraction, and composition thresholds necessary to nucleate these precipitates, and whether these effects are universally detrimental across different HEA chemistries.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of an as-cast single-phase high-entropy alloy. Subject one batch to accelerated aging by exposing it to service-relevant temperatures (e.g., 750 °C) and cyclic loading for a period sufficient to promote potential nanoscale segregation. Retain the second batch as a baseline. After treatment, perform standardized toughness tests (such as Charpy impact or fracture toughness measurements) and detailed microstructural characterization (using transmission electron microscopy and atom probe tomography) to search for nanoscale precipitates.
measurements: TEM/atom-probe imaging to detect nanoscale precipitate presence and distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no statistically significant reduction in toughness is observed in the aged/cycled samples compared to the baseline—and microstructural analyses do not reveal the emergence of nanoscale brittle precipitates—the hypothesis that localized segregation-induced precipitation governs brittle behavior in initially single-phase HEAs will be falsified.
